commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether prespecifying subgroup analyses and enrolling enough patients per subgroup produces more accurate fairness findings; eight sources endorse the practice on reasoning and consensus. Three hazard studies show that small subgroups, sometimes with fewer than 10 cases or a minimum size of 1, yield unstable subgroup estimates.

perspectives.view: No study compares prespecified, adequately powered subgroup analyses with post hoc or underpowered ones, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The three hazard studies are level 4 and 5 offline evaluations. They are consistent in showing imprecise subgroup estimates when counts are small, but they do not test the remedy.

In one tuberculosis chest X-ray evaluation, 58 cases in total left some subgroups with fewer than 10 cases. That pattern suggests a model could underperform in a group without the evaluation detecting it, and the failure would then surface only after deployment.

In an ICU cohort of 10,038 older adults, estimates for Black, Asian, and Hispanic patients were highly unstable because samples were small. In another benchmark, intersectional subgroups fell to 1 or 2 patients. Groups that are already underrepresented may be the ones whose disparities go unmeasured.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks for a subgroup analysis plan in marketing submissions. The CHAI playbooks ask for minimum sample sizes and subgroup requirements in validation documents. Both are recommendations drawn from consensus and do not rest on outcome evidence for the practice.

The hazard studies suggest that total sample size does not guarantee subgroup adequacy. One benchmark drew on 7,168 records and still had intersectional cells of 1 or 2 patients. Meeting per-subgroup targets may require targeted enrollment or multisite data, and the cost of that effort has not been measured.

commentary.research_gap: No study has compared prespecified, adequately powered subgroup analyses with post hoc or underpowered analyses. Such a study would ask whether prespecification changes the detection or accuracy of disparities, and what enrollment it would take to power intersectional subgroups.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The hazard studies did not report these populations either, although one covered older adults and flagged small racial and ethnic subgroups. Evidence on whether the practice protects these groups is absent.
